verses.text: On that day, King Ahasuerus gave the house of Haman, the Jews’ enemy, to Esther the queen. Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he was to her.
The king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and begged him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews.
Then the king held out to Esther the golden scepter. So Esther arose, and stood before the king.

She said, “If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and the thing seem right to the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the king’s provinces.
For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people? How can I endure to see the destruction of my relatives?”
Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, “See, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and him they have hanged on the gallows, because he laid his hand on the Jews.

Write also to the Jews, as it pleases you, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring; for the writing which is written in the king’s name, and sealed with the king’s ring, may not be reversed by any man.”

Then the king’s scribes were called at that time, in the third month, which is the month Sivan, on the twenty-third day of the month; and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded to the Jews, and to the satraps, and the governors and princes of the provinces which are from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces, to every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language, and to the Jews in their writing, and in their language.
He wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus, and sealed it with the king’s ring, and sent letters by courier on horseback, riding on royal horses that were bred from swift steeds.

In those letters, the king granted the Jews who were in every city to gather themselves together, and to defend their life, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all the power of the people and province that would assault them, their little ones and women, and to plunder their possessions,
on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.
A copy of the letter, that the decree should be given out in every province, was published to all the peoples, that the Jews should be ready for that day to avenge themselves on their enemies.
So the couriers who rode on royal horses went out, hastened and pressed on by the king’s commandment. The decree was given out in the citadel of Susa.
Mordecai went out of the presence of the king in royal clothing of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a robe of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa shouted and was glad.
The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor.

In every province, and in every city, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast, and a good day. Many from among the peoples of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews was fallen on them.

footnotes.content: The king rewarded Esther's courage with Haman's own house. Notice how Providence moves quietly: Esther revealed her identity because she loved her people more than her safety, and the king responded with justice. That's how the Lord works—through faithful hearts, He reverses what seemed sealed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's ring—the very instrument Haman used to write death—now sealed authority into Mordecai's hands. Esther managed the estate. One man's wickedness became another's redemption, all through the king's yes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther fell at the king's feet again, weeping not for herself but for her people. Tears born of love for others have a power that self-pity can never touch. She asked not for favor but for reversal—to undo the harm Haman had devised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The golden scepter extended—a sign of the king's willingness to hear. Esther rose to her feet with courage, knowing her tears had been received. Sometimes the Lord opens a door by the smallest gesture of welcome.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther's petition was layered with humility—'if it pleases,' 'if I have found favor,' 'if it seem right.' Yet her request was clear and bold: reverse the letters of death. She knew how to ask without demanding, to speak truth with grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The question she asked—'How can I endure?'—moved the king's heart because it spoke the deepest truth. She could not watch her people destroyed. That's what love looks like: it cannot stand idle while others perish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king declared what he had already done—given Esther the house, executed Haman. Then he said, 'Because he laid his hand on the Jews.' Justice has a long memory, and so does the Lord. He sees every hand raised against His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king gave Esther and Mordecai his seal—the power to write in his name. A decree sealed with the king's ring could not be reversed. What seemed impossible was now given into faithful hands to write mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Speed and reach: the scribes called in the third month, writing to one hundred twenty-seven provinces, in every language and writing. God's purposes do not move slowly when the moment comes. From India to Ethiopia, the word went out—reversal was coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Royal horses, swift steeds, couriers riding hard. The kingdom's resources were mobilized to carry salvation instead of death. What machinery of power will the Lord command when it serves His people's deliverance?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The decree granted the Jews the right to defend themselves, to stand against 'all the power' of those who would assault them. This was not vengeance born of pride—it was the dignity of self-preservation, of refusing to be destroyed without resistance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thirteenth day of Adar—the very day Haman had chosen for their destruction. Now it was appointed for their defense. The Lord did not change the date; He changed whose hand held the power on that day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A copy published in every province—so all peoples would know the Jews were ready, prepared, waiting to avenge themselves. Fear, once a weapon against them, now became armor: the peoples knew what was written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The couriers hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment. From Susa's citadel, the decree went forth. There is always a center of power, and on this day it moved toward life instead of death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai dressed in royal colors—blue, white, gold, fine linen, purple. The orphan boy became the man in the palace. Susa shouted and was glad; they saw that the exile's nephew had risen to honor. The city knew that the tide had turned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Light, gladness, joy, honor—four words that gather what the Jews felt in that hour. Readers today hear an echo of what any people know when deliverance comes: not just survival, but the restoration of dignity and joy that was taken from them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gladness, joy, feasting, good days—and many from the peoples became Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them. When God's people stand with dignity, others turn toward them. The feast became the seed of faith; fear became the doorway to conversion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
